name: dudo-core
description: Dudo-Core — deployment tooling for the Cloudflare Worker. See wrangler.jsonc.

scripts.//typecheck: Both trees. `packages/testing` was checked by NOTHING until 2026-09-05, which concealed a fixture that had silently stopped composing what production composes while 400+ assertions kept passing — the suites reported on a shape the product no longer had. The gate landed red with 14 diagnostics and was deliberately kept OUT of this script until it was green, because a red gate folded into a green one makes the green one worthless. It is green as of 2026-09-05 and is now part of the gate. Three of the original 14 were exactly the drift it was added to catch.
scripts.typecheck: npm run typecheck:core && npm run typecheck:tests
scripts.//check:contracts: RETIRED 2026-09-05, the same day it was added, and deliberately not by deleting a check. Unsatisfiable request shapes — a `required` field absent from `properties` under `additionalProperties: false` — are now asserted by `packages/testing/suites/contracts/satisfiability.ts`, which is `qa-agent`'s and is strictly richer: same walk, plus a proof that the walker descends into nested `properties`/`items`/`allOf`, plus a mirror control proving it does not flag everything. `architecture.md` §1 assigns the shape — *producer and consumer are both tested against the contract by `qa-agent`* — and this was a test wearing root tooling's clothes. Retired by this repository's own rule for duplicate checks: two checks are both worth keeping only when each would go red on an input the other passes, and this one would not. It found four real defects first, including `login-v1`'s, which is why the suite case exists at all.
scripts.//test: The four suite entry points. Added 2026-09-05 after `qa-agent` pointed out that NOTHING invoked `packages/testing/**` — `typecheck:tests` only TYPE-checks it. So the suites, the six negative controls, the type-negative probe, every registry-coherence check and the contract-satisfiability case were reachable only by an agent typing their paths, and the contract check had just been moved OUT of `typecheck` on the argument that a suite case runs more often than root tooling. That argument was backwards and this script is what makes it true. All four set a non-zero exit code on failure, so it gates correctly. `run-az2-timing.ts` is DELIBERATELY ABSENT and is not an oversight: it is a measurement rather than a test, and its own header records why — a wall-clock threshold on a shared laptop fails for reasons unrelated to the code, and a suite that goes red under load teaches a team to ignore red. The structural proof of equal work lives in `suites/az2-login/equal-work.ts` and holds on any machine.
scripts.test: node packages/testing/run-platform-operator.ts && node packages/testing/run-customer-directory.ts && node packages/testing/run-az2-login.ts && node packages/testing/run-type-negative.ts
scripts.//migrations: LOCAL variants act on the local simulated D1 and are safe to run freely. REMOTE variants act on the deployed database and are a production-class action requiring explicit user approval each time (.claude/rules/security.md §7). They are separate scripts, and named, so neither can be run by accident.
scripts.//deploy: There is no `deploy` script, deliberately. Deployment is gated on C5 and on explicit user approval; a one-word npm script is exactly the wrong affordance for an action that needs a decision.
